subject: Private ingress route evaluation: peering vs endpoint proxy vs encrypted tunnel
messages:
From: Ryan Cole <ryan@acme-analytics.com>
To: Chloe Martin <chloe.martin@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Cc: Bethany Li <bethany@acme-analytics.com>

Subject: Evaluating connection options for our private deployment (peering/endpoint/VPN)

Hi Chloe / Marissa —

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. As we start scoping our Private deployment I wanted a short sanity-check on connectivity options before we lock anything into our network team. Our primary goals are: low predictable latency for inference, tenant isolation for PII workloads, and minimal ops overhead for our infra team.

We're currently considering three patterns:
- Direct VPC peering from our prod VPC to Redwood's dedicated VPC
- Endpoint/proxy model (PrivateLink-style) where we call through an endpoint service and keep all traffic through managed endpoints
- Site-to-site IPSec VPN with egress IP allowlists back to your host layer

Attached is a rough network diagram and our initial security checklist. Can you call out major pros/cons you see from a Redwood operational perspective and any hard constraints we should expect (SLA, bandwidth, cross-AZ limits, egress pricing)? Would also appreciate a recommended default for a greenfield deployment and a suggested rollout path if we want to minimize blast radius.

Attachments: network-diagram-peering-vs-endpoint.pdf (diagram), acme-security-checklist.xlsx (referenced)

Ryan

Head of Cloud Infrastructure | Acme Analytics
ryan@acme-analytics.com

Subject: Re: Evaluating connection options for our private deployment (peering/endpoint/VPN)

Ryan — thanks for the clear ask and the diagram, that helps. High level summary first, then a suggested rollout: 

High-level pros/cons (short):
- VPC peering: simplest networking model, lowest added latency, but scales poorly for multi-account topologies and you lose the ability to do cross-account PrivateLink-style security boundaries. Peering also requires route management and can increase blast radius when peering to large production VPCs.
- Endpoint/proxy (PrivateLink-like): best isolation (explicit service endpoints), easier to grant per-service access, limited surface area for egress controls. Slightly more operational overhead and potential for per-connection throughput limits depending on provider quotas. Works well when you want fine-grained access control and auditability.
- Site-to-site VPN: good for customers who cannot or will not do peering or endpoints (on-prem or restricted networks). Easier for air-gapped or legacy networks but typically higher and less predictable latency; needs lifecycle management (IPSec rotations, monitoring) and generally not our recommended steady-state for high-throughput inference.

Suggested rollout for greenfield (minimize blast radius):
1) Start with PrivateLink-style endpoints for control plane and initial inferencing routes (keeps isolation and allows gradual scaling).
2) Validate latency on representative traffic (we can provide a perf harness for 95th/99th percentile.)
3) If you need the absolute lowest tail latency and can tolerate broader routing, add a peering connection between a dedicated peering VPC and your prod VPC for high-throughput workloads; keep sensitive workloads on endpoints.
4) Reserve VPN as fallback/DR for regional failover or for on-prem sites that cannot use AWS endpoints.

Notes / constraints from Redwood:
- SLA: endpoint model supports our standard latency SLO in most regions; peering can improve tail latency but requires cross-account routing approvals.
- Bandwidth: if you plan sustained multi-GPU throughput (>10Gbps sustained), peering is usually simpler to operate but check cloud provider cross-account bandwidth quotas.
- Auditing: PrivateLink gives clearer per-connection attribution in our logs; peering requires VPC flow logs + correlation.

I'll loop Karthik (networking) for a short writeup with expected changes to routing table, required peering permissions, and a recommended security group/NACL baseline. If you'd like, we can run a shortpilot for 72 hours with synthetic traffic to collect real tail latency numbers.

Attachment: network-diagram-peering-vs-endpoint.pdf (annotated)

Ryan — quick operational notes from my side:
- Provisioning time: endpoint model ~2 business days to configure for a single region once subnets/security groups are agreed; peering can be instant on our side but often blocked by customer networking approvals and routing reviews (so plan for 3–10 business days).
- Cost: endpoints have per-hour and per-GB charges (provider dependent); peering has no per-connection charge but may increase egress bill and you should model traffic.
- Ops: VPN requires certificate/IPSec lifecycle; we provide a managed endpoint for the tunnel but customer will need on-prem firewall rules and rotation policy for long term.

If you want, we can start with the endpoint proxy for the first week so you can run canary traffic while our networking team prepares a peering runbook. That gives you isolation and a known rollback path.

Marissa

Ryan / team — adding the network-team perspective and an actionable checklist. Apologies for the late reply; wanted to include tests and concrete config snippets.

Short recommendation: Start with endpoint/service-proxy for initial onboarding + production small-scale traffic. After 1–2 weeks of production telemetry, move to a dedicated peering path for high-throughput, latency-sensitive workloads. Keep endpoints for control-plane and sensitive PII workloads. Reserve VPN for on-prem sites or where security policy disallows endpoints/peering.

Checklist & config notes:
- Endpoint path (PrivateLink-style):
  * Required: create VPC endpoint service on Redwood side, customer creates interface endpoints in their VPC subnets.
  * Subnet sizing: endpoints need at least two /28s in different AZs to be resilient.
  * Security: SG on endpoint should allow only customer CIDRs and Redwood management CIDR.
  * Monitoring: enable flow logs + our agent; set up per-endpoint metrics with 1m granularity.
  * Quotas: request increases for ENI limits if you plan >50 concurrent endpoints per AZ.

- Peering path:
  * Required: peering between a dedicated Redwood peering VPC and customer VPC; update route tables and ensure no overlapping CIDRs.
  * NACLs/Security: follow least-privilege, restrict to required ports (TLS on inference ports).
  * Multi-account: use transitive routing only with approved transit gateways (avoid transitive on standard peering).
  * Validation: we will provide a perf harness to run 95/99th latency checks across AZs for 24–72 hours.

- VPN path:
  * Required: IPSec connection with pre-shared key or certificate options.
  * Ops: schedule quarterly key rotations and integrate with customer firewall change windows.
  * Performance: test with jumbo frames disabled initially; check MTU/path MTU across hops.

Rollout proposal (concrete steps):
1) Week 0: Endpoint provisioning + 24-hour synthetic perf.
2) Week 1–2: Ingest small production traffic (10–20% of traffic) to endpoint.
3) Week 2–3: Configure peering in parallel (routing approvals from customer).
4) Week 3: Gradual shift of high-throughput workloads to peering VPC, keep endpoints for PII.

I'll attach a short template for route table entries and an ENI quota checklist if you'd like; happy to join a call with your network/security folks tomorrow.
